D4D semantic evaluation • v8 only • primary ratings

Completeness, review concerns, and source relationships

Historical cohort: September 2026. These reports describe frozen generic-v7/v8 records and their September 12 CBORG reference rescore, not the current generator or a current validation of its outputs. Saved render metadata dates v7 to September 1–2 and v8 to September 5 (VOICE replicate 1) or September 7 (the other 11 records). Labels beginning 2026-09-04f/g are run identifiers, not the generation dates of all v8 records. Provenance recording timestamps are distinct from exact model-call start times; see the saved VOICE v8 replicate 1 and CM4AI v8 replicate 2 records.

CM4AI generation-regime caveat. V8 replicates 2 and 3 returned no thinking block in the full, reconciliation, report, and report re-check phases. The historical requests omitted the thinking parameter; the generation analysis documents an input-correlated adaptive outcome, not an explicit request to disable thinking or an established proxy fault. Both replicate 2 and replicate 3 remain included in every original score and pooled result. The pooled CM4AI comparison therefore mixes observed thinking regimes. This limits attribution of differences to the v8 package alone; it does not establish that the regime explains any score difference or justify a corrected score.

Measurements recomputed for the 12 v8 datasheets: AI_READI, CHORUS, CM4AI, and VOICE, each with three generation replicates and one retained primary evaluation under each rubric. No evaluations were rerun.

Main findings

  • AI_READI and VOICE have the highest mean recorded scores under both rubrics; CHORUS has the lowest. The rubrics assess different constructs, so their percentages should be read separately.
  • Consistency (105) and completeness (100) account for 205 of 303 comments (67.7%). There are also 36 content-accuracy, 29 correctness, and 33 semantic-understanding comments.
  • Among 12 fields selected by v8 absent-field mentions, 106 of 144 record–field pairs are structurally absent; 62 of those absences are mentioned in completeness comments. These selected-field counts are not an overall completeness rate.
  • All 12 records have at least one accuracy or correctness flag. The most frequently implicated root is source_caveats (10/12 records); this often reflects a source conflict recorded in the datasheet, rather than an independently established extraction error.
  • Source associations differ by dataset and outcome. For example, documentation-linked fields have a +17.6 percentage-point completeness-flag contrast in CM4AI and −15.7 in VOICE. These descriptive contrasts do not identify source effects.
Interpretation qualification. Seven of the 12 rubric20 evaluations have identified Q19 rationale qualifications; selected CM4AI Q13/version interpretations also need adjudication. Scores below preserve the recorded evaluations. Native “accuracy” and “correctness” labels are review allegations, not verified factual-error rates.

Section scoring and negative comments by input-document type

This view pools all 12 v8 records, without separate program or dataset panels. Columns identify the types of documents supplied with each record. A record can appear in several columns because its input bundle contains several document types. Pooling does not statistically adjust for dataset; these are overlapping observational groups.

The three views answer different questions: how many section comments occur when a document family is available; how selected section-related rubric10 items score in those records; and how often the fields actually linked to that document family are flagged. They should not be interpreted as measuring the same outcome.

Read the columns as input-bundle profiles, not document rankings. Docs and Awards both occur in all 12 records, so their availability-based columns necessarily match. Publications, Repositories, and Terms also identify the same nine records and therefore have identical availability-based profiles. Structured and Tutorials each represent only one dataset. The receipt-linked view uses different field subsets and can differ even when the available-record cohorts are identical.

Where negative comments concentrate

Across all 12 records, Composition and Metadata each receive 11.4 section-tagged issue entries per record on average, followed by Data Governance (4.5), FileCollection (4.0), and Human (4.0). This is review burden, not a normalized error rate: larger sections provide more opportunities for comments, and the two rubrics can repeat a concern.

Selected section-related scores

Using the all-record cohort, the selected Variables item averages 50%, the Preprocessing item 75%, and the three Maintenance items 77.8%. Collection, Distribution, Motivation, and Uses average 100% on their selected items despite receiving negative comments. Binary rubric10 criteria and detailed semantic comments measure different things; a full item score does not certify an entire section as correct.

Comments on fields linked to each document family

This narrower view uses receipt support rather than input availability. It describes the reviewed fields associated with a source family, while retaining the section context.

Limits on claims. These data support statements about observed section profiles in v8 input bundles. They do not show that adding a document type changes scores or reduces comments independently of the dataset. No significance tests are added: overlapping cohorts, only four dataset contexts, and source types tied to individual datasets limit such inference. The source grouping, record-level denominators, included/excluded score items, and unrounded native-type estimates are exported for inspection.

Do section differences persist after accounting for size?

Yes, differences remain after normalizing scoring opportunities, but the leading sections depend on the measure and dataset. The analysis below separates each section’s loss rate from its contribution to total score loss. It also tests three field denominators for negative comments. These are arithmetic normalizations, not a fitted model of dataset-independent section effects.

Score-loss rate versus contribution

Across the 12 v8 records, rubric10 loses 76 of 591 applicable points (12.9%). Metadata accounts for the most lost points among mapped sections: 17 points, or 22.4% of all loss. Its normalized loss rate is 17/108 = 15.7%. Variables loses fewer points overall (6, or 7.9% of total loss), but has the largest normalized rate: 6/12 = 50%. Preprocessing loses 3/12 (25%) and Maintenance 8/36 (22.2%).

The crosswalk is partial. The existing 39-item rubric10 mapping explains 54 of the 76 lost points. The remaining 22 lost points (28.9%) belong to 11 unmapped items and appear as a separate row. Variables, Preprocessing, and several other sections have only one mapped item per record. FileCollection has none. These are selected-item section profiles, not complete section scores; rubric20 deductions are not allocated here.

Negative-comment concentration after field-count normalization

Metadata and Composition each had 11.4 raw section comments per record. They separate after normalization: 36.4% versus 61.3% of mapped candidate record–field pairs are flagged. The corresponding populated-field rates are 37.6% versus 68.8%, and receipt-linked populated rates are 44.3% versus 69.5%. Thus Composition has more concentrated root-level criticism than Metadata under all three definitions, despite equal raw comment counts.

Root count is only one measure of section size. FileCollection and Variables each have one mapped root that may contain many nested entries. Their high flag proportions cannot establish higher error density per nested field, claim, file, or word. Candidate denominators include optional fields; populated and linked denominators hide omissions. None is a verified applicable-field denominator.

Consistency across records and datasets

The table below also compares each section’s normalized loss with the other mapped sections in the same record, and recomputes section loss after omitting each dataset in turn. This checks whether a pooled result is driven by a particular dataset without treating the 12 generations as independent datasets.

The document-family table applies the same field-count normalization to the input-availability cohorts used in Figure 9. All 14 native document types, completeness-only and accuracy/correctness flags, record-level denominators, and paired score comparisons are exported in the linked JSON tables. The already-normalized receipt-linked family view in Figure 11 averages records equally; this sensitivity table pools record–field pairs, weighting records by the number of eligible fields.

Supported conclusion: In this v8 evaluation, selected rubric10 items associated with Variables have a higher pooled proportion of scoring points lost than those associated with Metadata, although Metadata contributes more lost points overall. Composition has a higher flagged-root proportion than Metadata under all three field definitions. Neither result establishes a universal section ranking or a section effect independent of dataset, item difficulty, rubric coverage, or nested content size.

Methods, sensitivity, and reproducibility

All figures use v8 primary ratings only. No v7 observations, repeat ratings, pooled-cohort p-values, or pooled manual-adjudication sample rates enter this report. The 840 item records comprise 50 rubric10 subelements and 20 rubric20 questions per datasheet. Reported score means give each generation replicate equal weight.

The three generations per dataset share a dataset and source context. They do not provide three independent dataset samples. With only four datasets and sparse, unequal source comparisons, this report emphasizes observed variation and effect sizes; it does not add inferential significance tests. Selected missing fields and accuracy roots are exploratory, chosen using these same v8 observations.

The 2,556 retained receipt links include 38 links to structurally unpopulated roots. Figure 7 retains declared links; Figure 8 restricts its comparison universe to populated roots. The latter can therefore miss omission problems involving entirely absent fields. Source availability, field selection, topic difficulty, and review behavior remain possible explanations for the observed contrasts.

Cross-rubric overlap below measures agreement in flagged field sets, not reviewer reliability or factual validity. Removing Q19, or Q13 and Q19, is an item-omission sensitivity analysis, not a corrected score or an adjudication. Historical schema conventions matter: a bare DOI can be valid, and a landing page does not necessarily satisfy a direct download_url.

Search the 303 v8 review comments

Original review descriptions and recommendations are reproduced for inspection. They remain reviewer claims; recommendations have not been automatically adopted.

303 comments

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · consistency · medium

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:1 | Fields: sensitive_elements, confidential_elements, regulatory_restrictions.confidentiality_level, participant_privacy.privacy_techniques, future_use_impacts

sensitive_elements_present: false and confidential_elements_present: false sit uneasily with regulatory_restrictions.confidentiality_level: restricted, HIPAA-oriented handling, static watermarking of released copies, verified-ID access gating and an acknowledged theoretical re-identification risk. A release that genuinely contains nothing sensitive or confidential would not normally require that control stack; the two blocks appear to answer the healthsheet's narrow questions rather than characterise the release as governed.

Reviewer recommendation: Qualify sensitive_elements/confidential_elements to state that the released variables are not themselves sensitive while the release remains access-controlled because of residual re-identification risk, so the two claims are read together rather than as a contradiction.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · consistency · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:2 | Fields: is_deidentified.method, is_deidentified.deidentification_details, source_caveats

is_deidentified carries three mutually inconsistent source statements: FAIRhub records 'NoDeIdentification' (no identifiers collected), the RO-Crate records the release as deidentified, and the Nature Metabolism comment describes HIPAA Safe Harbor stripping. The structured method field asserts the strongest of the three (HIPAA Safe Harbor) while deidentification_details reports all three unreconciled.

Reviewer recommendation: State which statement the project treats as authoritative for the released files, or record the method as 'Safe Harbor verification, no identifiers collected' so the structured value and the prose do not diverge.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · completeness · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:3 | Fields: download_url, page, data_governance.access_review_process, external_resources

No download_url field is populated. The download route is nevertheless reconstructable from page, data_governance.access_review_process (verified-ID login, T2DM-only attestation, license assent) and the external resource https://fairhub.io/datasets/3/access, so the sub-element's purpose is met by platform access instructions rather than by a direct link.

Reviewer recommendation: Populate download_url with https://fairhub.io/datasets/3 or the access endpoint so machine clients can resolve the retrieval route without parsing prose.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · consistency · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:4 | Fields: distribution_formats, conforms_to, conforms_to_standard, file_collections.conforms_to

distribution_formats lists DICOM, CSV, JSON and Markdown, but the release also distributes WFDB electrocardiography records, Open mHealth wearable/CGM payloads and NASA ESDS-style ASCII environmental files per conforms_to and file_collections. The distribution list is narrower than the standards list, and no character encoding is stated anywhere.

Reviewer recommendation: Add distribution_formats entries for WFDB and the Open mHealth/ESDS text payloads with their media types, and record character encoding (e.g. UTF-8) for the text-based collections.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · semantic_understanding · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:5 | Fields: is_tabular, description, file_collections.clinical_data

is_tabular: false while the description states the modalities 'encompass tabular data, imaging data and physiological signal/waveform data' and clinical_data is distributed as one-to-one OMOP CDM CSV tables. The flag is defensible for a multimodal release that is not a single table, but read alone it contradicts the description.

Reviewer recommendation: Note beside is_tabular that the release is multimodal and that tabular content is confined to the OMOP clinical_data collection and participants.tsv.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · completeness · medium

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:6 | Fields: preprocessing_strategies, cleaning_strategies, external_resources, collection_mechanisms

No software that produced or transformed the released data is named. Conversion of Topcon .fda and FLIO .sdt exports to DICOM, of Garmin .FIT to Open mHealth, and mapping of clinical data to OMOP CDM are described as having happened, but no tool, package, version or repository is attached to any of those steps, and no used_software is recorded on preprocessing_strategies or cleaning_strategies. The software that is named occupies non-qualifying roles: REDCap and the MoCA Duo application are capture instrumentation; FAIRhub on Microsoft Azure is hosting; the OMOP CDM Data Quality Dashboard is validation of the released data; https://github.com/AI-READI is an organisation root that identifies the publisher rather than a piece of software.

Reviewer recommendation: Name the converters and mapping pipelines (tool name, version, and the AI-READI repository that holds each) on preprocessing_strategies.used_software so a reader can tell what produced the distributed DICOM, OMOP and Open mHealth files.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · completeness · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:7 | Fields: variables, source_caveats, conforms_to

variables provides 20 measures with name, data type, unit, description and measurement technique, but no ontology or concept identifiers (LOINC, OMOP concept_id, SNOMED) are attached, and source_caveats records that the authoritative per-domain data dictionary at docs.aireadi.org was not consulted. Variable coverage is therefore illustrative rather than exhaustive for a 356,343-file multimodal release.

Reviewer recommendation: Attach concept identifiers to each variable and link the released participants.json / per-domain data dictionary as the authoritative variable reference.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · completeness · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:8 | Fields: errata, data_protection_impacts, updates.update_details, version_access.version_details

No errata block and no data_protection_impacts (DPIA) block. Change information is instead carried by updates.update_details and version_access.version_details, and data-protection reasoning by participant_privacy and ethical_reviews, so both sub-elements are satisfied through their alternative fields rather than left undocumented.

Reviewer recommendation: Add an errata list (empty with a statement if none are known) and a short DPIA record referencing the re-identification analysis already present in future_use_impacts.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · content_accuracy · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:9 | Fields: creators.principal_investigator.affiliation, data_governance.accountable_organization, ethical_reviews.reviewing_organization, source_caveats

Institutional attribution is internally contradictory across the record: Washington University in St. Louis is named as licensor, accountable organization and PI affiliation, while the reviewing IRB, the award recipient per NIH RePORTER and the assay laboratory are all University of Washington. The record discloses the conflict in source_caveats rather than resolving it, which is honest but leaves accountable_organization pointing at an institution that no human-subjects or award evidence supports.

Reviewer recommendation: Resolve the attribution with the project, or mark accountable_organization as reported-by-FAIRhub and name the University of Washington as the human-subjects and award institution.

AI_READI_v8_rep1 · R10 · consistency · low

AI_READI_v8_rep1_r10_rating1:10 | Fields: collection_timeframes.source_caveats, license, source_caveats

Collection start is given as 2023-07-19 in collection_timeframes and the description while the BMJ Open protocol states 18 July 2023; license naming differs between two tier-1 sources ('AI-READI custom license v2.0' in the API, 'Health Data License' on the dataset page); a healthsheet answer describing first-year coverage contradicts the stated 2023-07-19 to 2025-05-01 window. All three are disclosed and adjudicated by source tier rather than left silent.

Reviewer recommendation: Retain the tier adjudication; where the project can confirm a single value upstream, cite the confirmation so downstream consumers stop inheriting the ambiguity.

AI_READI_v8_rep2 · R10 · completeness · medium

AI_READI_v8_rep2_r10_rating1:1 | Fields: preprocessing_strategies, cleaning_strategies, machine_annotation_tools, external_resources

No software that produced or transformed the distributed data is named. preprocessing_strategies states that Topcon .fda and Heidelberg .sdt exports were 'converted to DICOM', Garmin .FIT 'converted to the Open mHealth standard', ECG 'converted to WFDB', and that clinical data were 'mapped to' the OMOP CDM, but no converter, mapper or pipeline is identified; processing is described only as 'a combination of automated and custom processing'. The named software in the record occupies non-qualifying roles: REDCap and the MoCA Duo application are capture, FAIRhub on Microsoft Azure is hosting, the OMOP CDM Data Quality Dashboard is validation, and https://github.com/AI-READI is an organization root that identifies the publisher rather than a tool.

Reviewer recommendation: Name the conversion and OMOP-mapping software with versions and repository or DOI links (for example the specific .fda/.sdt-to-DICOM converters and the FIT-to-Open-mHealth tooling), attaching them via used_software on preprocessing_strategies.

Reviewer recommendation: Add distribution_formats entries for the internal formats of each archive (e.g. OME-TIFF/PNG for IF images, TSV/CSV for MS tables, MTX/H5AD for perturb-seq matrices) alongside the ZIP container.
